While estimates for predictors relatively stable with the inclusion of newer predictors, the estimate for the intercept increases between models. Additionally, younger passengers appear to have had a higher rate of survival, though the estimate for age is considerably lower than those of other variables.

title: 9041 Assignment 4
text:
Findings and Limitations
The findings of the full (and preferred) model match expectations based on what we know of emergency procedures of the time. For instance, men had a drastically lower odds of surviving than women such that men had 0.08 times the odds of surviving. This makes sense since culture and protocol at the time was to prioritize women and children first over men in evacuations. In the same vein, this may also help explain why younger passengers had greater survivorship where every 1 year of a passenger’s age was associated with 0.96 odds of surviving. Thus, this protocol of “women and children” on lifeboats/rafts first may play a large role in answering who survived the titanic since (to my recollection), the rate of survival for those who did not make it onto a raft was nearly none. Furthermore, it is unsurprising that ticket class affected rate of survival. In this case, those of lower ticket classes than first class such as second or third class ticket holders had dramatically lower rates of survival. This would support, though not necessarily confirm the hypothesis that first-class ticket holders had greater odds of survival due to better access to evacuation and emergency protocol and equipment. More hypothetically, since ticket class is likely associated with SES, it is also possible that those of higher education and wealth may have had greater personal knowledge and access to lifesaving measures. Put together, the model comparisons suggest that all three (i.e., sex, class, age) are notable predictors of surviving the Titanic. While there are likely more predictors at play, these three predictors of sex, class, and age very likely play a large part in determining who survives. Nonetheless, it is possible that the interpretation of these predictors in our current models and estimates don’t fully capture their effects and nuances. For example, here, we examine age in a linear fashion, without capturing the nuance of a potential non-linear relationship with survivorship. For instance, it may be possible that infants and children under 10 or 11 may have drastically lower survival rates similar to the elderly. Though in this case, all our model and estimates can capture is that survival decreases as age increases - which could be an inaccurate statement if the relationship is skewed. It would therefore be pertinent to investigate potential nuances with age as a predictor of survival, and also look into potential interactions between sex, class, and other factors.

title: Binary Logistic Regression
text:
This report demonstrates a complete binary logistic regression workflow. We will use the couples dataset from class.
Our objectives are to:

Specify and estimate several plausible competing binary logistic regression models using glmmTMB.
Compare nested models using likelihood-ratio tests (χ²).
Evaluate overall model fit using AIC and BIC.
Examine model diagnostics and assess assumptions relevant to binary logistic regression.
Select and interpret a preferred model, including transforming log-odds coefficients into odds ratios.
Report results reproducibly using tables, figures, and Quarto.

section: 1. Load packages and prepare the data
text:
1. Load packages and prepare the data
Install any missing packages once in the R Console:
install.packages(c(
  "glmmTB", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2",
  "broom.mixed", "performance", "gt", 
  "DHARMa", "ggeffects"))
The following code belongs in the Quarto document.


Code
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)

couples <- read_csv("data/couples.csv")

n <- nrow(couples)


The dataset contains information about couples’ relationship status (stayed), relationship satisfaction scores (satisfaction), attachment avoidance scores (avoidance), and cohabitation status (cohabiting).

Research Question and Predictions
How are avoidance, satisfaction, and cohabiting associated with whether couples stayed together?
We expect:

Couples with higher relationship satisfaction scores are more likely to stay together.
Couples with lower attachment avoidance scores are more likely to stay together.
Couples who cohabit (live together) are more likely to stay together.

These are predictions about associations, not causal effects.

title: Binary Logistic Regression
text:
3. Specify and estimate competing models
We will fit an intercept-only model and three increasingly complex substantive models.








Model
Formula
Research rationale




mod0: Null
stayed ~ 1
Baseline model


mod1: Satisfaction
stayed ~ satisfaction
Staying together varies with relationship satisfaction


mod2: Satisfaction + Avoidance
stayed ~ satisfaction + avoidance
Avoidant attachment explains additional variation


mod3: Satisfaction + Avoidance + Cohabiting
stayed ~ satisfactoin + avoidance + cohabiting
Cohabiting explains additional variation



The models are nested: each successive model contains all predictors from the preceding model, plus one or more additional predictors.


Code
mod0 <- glmmTMB(stayed ~ 1,data = couples,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  stayed ~ satisfaction,
  data = couples,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  stayed ~ satisfaction + avoidance,
  data = couples,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  stayed ~ satisfaction + avoidance + cohabiting,
  data = couples,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))


After executing the model-fitting code, explore the results in the R Console:
summary(mod0)
summary(mod1)
summary(mod2)
summary(mod3)

confint(mod3)

title: Binary Logistic Regression
text:
4. Nested Model Comparisons
We will evaluate the models. Our main performance metrics are:

AIC: Evaluates model fit while penalizing model complexity. Lower values indicate a preferred balance between fit and complexity.
BIC: Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity. Lower values are preferred.
Likelihood-ratio test (χ²): Tests whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit relative to the preceding model. A statistically significant p-value (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictors improve model fit.


4.1. Compare the models
Because our models are nested and estimated using the same observations, we can compare all four models in a single anova() call.


Code
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

tests


Data: couples
Models:
mod0: stayed ~ 1, zi=~0, disp=~1
mod1: stayed ~ satisfaction, zi=~0, disp=~1
mod2: stayed ~ satisfaction + avoidance, zi=~0, disp=~1
mod3: stayed ~ satisfaction + avoidance + cohabiting, zi=~0, disp=~1

mod0  1 445.50 449.27 -221.75   443.50                              
mod1  2 402.98 410.52 -199.49   398.98 44.5174      1  2.521e-11 ***
mod2  3 395.36 406.66 -194.68   389.36  9.6276      1   0.001917 ** 
mod3  4 391.72 406.79 -191.86   383.72  5.6382      1   0.017573 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Each row represents a model. We can retain and rename the statistics relevant to our comparison table.


Code
tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)




4.2. Extract overall model performance
The glance() function from the broom.mixed package returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics.
We can apply it to each fitted model.


Code
glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod0)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod1)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod2)
glance3 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod3)


We can then combine these results using rbind().


Code
mods <- c(
  "mod0: Null",
  "mod1: Satisfaction",
  "mod2: + Avoidance",
  "mod3: + Cohabiting")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3)




4.3. Combine nested tests and model performance
Because the rows in glances and tests represent the same models in the same order, we can combine them using cbind().


Code
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)




4.4. Display the combined model comparison table


Code
comparison_table |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))

4.5. Interpreting the combined table
Each row represents one fitted binary logistic regression model.
When comparing models, we generally look for lower AIC and BIC values and whether the likelihood-ratio test indicates a statistically significant improvement in model fit.
For example, the mod2 row tells us how well mod2 fits the data relative to mod1, considering both model fit and complexity (AIC, BIC). The likelihood-ratio test is significant, telling us that adding avoidance as a predictor significantly improves model fit beyond satisfaction.
The mod3 comparison tests whether adding cohabitation significantly improves model fit after accounting for satisfaction and avoidance. For mod3, the likelihood-ratio test is significant, AIC is lower, however, BIC slightly increases. Given how minimally BIC increases, mod3 is our preferred model.
Remember: The mod0 row has no incremental comparison because it serves as the baseline.


Additional performance comparison
The performance package also provides a convenient way to compare fitted models.


Code
performance_comparison <- compare_performance(
  mod0,
  mod1,
  mod2,
  mod3,
  rank = TRUE)


In the Console, inspect:
performance_comparison
plot(performance_comparison)
These functions may include additional metrics, such as Tjur’s R2, which we will not focus on here.

title: Binary Logistic Regression
text:
5. Select a provisional model
Model selection requires considering both statistical evidence and model complexity.
In particular, we should consider:

Nested-model χ²-tests.
AIC.
BIC.
Model complexity.
Diagnostic findings.
Substantive interpretability.

For this demonstration, we will use the likelihood-ratio test as an initial selection criterion. We can see that the likelihood ratio test is still significant for our most complex model, mod3. Therefore we will select our model by filtering by Nested.p.value and using slice_tail() to extract the last row in our comparison table.


Code
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

#creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

#case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "mod0: Null" = mod0,
  "mod1: Satisfaction" = mod1,
  "mod2: + Avoidance" = mod2,
  "mod3: + Cohabiting" = mod3)


The provisionally selected model is mod3: + Cohabiting.
Its performance is:

AIC = 391.718
BIC = 406.792

We will now examine whether the selected model has important diagnostic problems.

title: Binary Logistic Regression
text:
6. Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics
Binary logistic regression diagnostics help identify potential violations of model assumptions and unusual observations.
Here, we will examine:

Linearity on the log-odds scale, not on the probability scale
No catastrophic collinearity
No complete separation
No influential outliers
Events per predictor


6.1 Linearity on the logit scale


Code
set.seed(10000)
res_mod3 <- simulateResiduals(mod3, n = 500, plot = FALSE)



The default DHARMa plot









When interpreting these plots, consider:
Q–Q plot

Do the residuals deviate substantially from a uniform distribution on the log-odds scale?

DHARMa residuals vs. predicted plot

Does residual variability change across fitted values on the log-odds scale?

Residuals versus leverage

Are there observations with unusually high leverage or influence?




6.2 Collinearity

6.3 Complete separation
We should not have predictor(s) that perfectly predict the outcome variable. Therefore, it is important to check for symptoms for this in your preferred model. The main symptom are:

Very large coefficients and standard errors
glmmTMBwarnings about convergence
Fitted probabilities of essentially 0 or 1 for some groups



6.4 Influence
Cook’s distance is not implemented for glmmTMB, so use the DHARMa again to check for outliers.


Code
testOutliers(res_mod3)

Here we have 163 together-couples and 157 dissolved-couples, with 3 coefficients in mod3.
These diagnostics should inform your final model selection. A model with slightly better fit statistics may not be preferable if its assumptions are seriously compromised. For the purposes of this worked example, we retain the provisionally selected model for the reporting demonstration.

title: Binary Logistic Regression
text:
8. Interpret the results

8.1. Coefficients are on the log-odds scale


Code
fixef(mod3)



Conditional model:
  (Intercept)   satisfaction      avoidance  cohabitingYes  
      -2.7690         0.8019        -0.4001         0.5916  


The coefficients represent changes in the log-odds of staying together at 12 months, holding the other predictors constant.
For a one-point increase in satisfaction, holding avoidance and cohabiting status constant, the log-odds of staying together increase by 0.8.
For a one-point increase in avoidance, holding satisfaction and cohabiting status constant, the log-odds of staying together decrease by 0.4.
The coefficient for cohabitingYes represents the log-odds difference between cohabiting and non-cohabiting couples, holding satisfaction and avoidance constant. Recall that not cohabiting is our reference group, therefore the log-odds of staying together increase by 0.59 when couples live together compared to when they do not , holding satisfaction and avoidance constant.


8.2 Transform log-odds into odds ratios
Exponentiating the coefficients transforms them from log-odds into odds ratios.


Code
exp(fixef(mod3)$cond)


  (Intercept)  satisfaction     avoidance cohabitingYes 
   0.06272427    2.22968481    0.67022271    1.80683201 


We can also exponentiate the confidence intervals to obtain 95% confidence intervals for the odds ratios.


Code
or_ci <- exp(confint(mod3, parm = "beta_"))
or_ci


                   2.5 %    97.5 %   Estimate
(Intercept)   0.01848829 0.2128014 0.06272427
satisfaction  1.75456494 2.8334627 2.22968481
avoidance     0.52859712 0.8497937 0.67022271
cohabitingYes 1.10304976 2.9596506 1.80683201




Interpreting satisfaction
Holding avoidance and cohabiting status constant, a one-point increase in satisfaction is associated with 2.23 times the odds of staying together at 12 months, 95% CI [1.75, 2.83].


Interpreting avoidance
Holding satisfaction and cohabiting status constant, a one-point increase in avoidance is associated with 0.67 times the odds of staying together at 12 months, 95% CI [0.53, 0.85].


Interpreting cohabiting
Holding satisfaction and avoidance constant, cohabiting couples have 1.81 times the odds of staying together at 12 months compared to non-cohabiting couples, 95% CI [1.1, 2.96].


8.3 Visualizing results as predicted probabilities
We can visualize the associations between our predictors and outcome variable using predicted probabilities, which can be calculated using ggeffects::ggpredict() and plotted using ggplot2.

Satisfaction


Code
pred_sat <- ggpredict(mod3, terms = "satisfaction [1:7 by=0.05]")

ggplot(pred_sat, aes(x, predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Relationship Satisfaction",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Staying Together"
  ) +
  theme_classic()











Avoidance


Code
pred_pclass <- ggpredict(mod3, terms = "avoidance [1:7 by=0.05]")

ggplot(pred_pclass, aes(x, predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Avoidance",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Staying Together"
  ) +
  theme_classic()












Results paragraph

We fit a binomial GLM with a logit link predicting 12-month relationship status from satisfaction, attachment avoidance, and cohabiting status. Higher satisfaction was associated with higher odds of remaining together, OR = 2.23, 95% CI [1.75, 2.83]. Higher attachment avoidance was associated with lower odds of remaining together, OR = 0.67, 95% CI [0.53, 0.85]. Cohabiting couples had higher odds of remaining together compared to non-cohabiting couples, OR = 1.81, 95% CI [1.1, 2.96].



Substantive conclusions
This analysis illustrates how relationship dissolution can be investigated using several competing binary logistic regression models.
The model-comparison process allows us to evaluate whether additional predictors explain meaningful variation beyond simpler models.
The final model provides estimates of the odds of a couple staying together or dissolving.

title: Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
In this lab, you will apply binary logistic regression analysis to investigate the factors associated with surviving the Titanic crash. Rather than estimating a single binary logistic regression model, you will develop and compare a series of competing models, evaluate their performance, examine binary logistic regression diagnostics, and interpret the results of your preferred model.
Your goal is to produce a reproducible statistical report that demonstrates not only how to estimate binary logistic regression models, but also how to make and justify decisions about model specification and selection.
You will complete the analysis in R, document your workflow in Quarto, and publish the rendered report using GitHub Pages.


By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Specify multiple binary logistic regression models based on substantive predictions.
Estimate and compare nested binary logistic regression models using AIC, BIC and likelihood-ratio tests.
Evaluate binary logistic regression assumptions and identify potentially influential observations.
Select a preferred model and justify that decision.
Extract, report, and interpret binary logistic regression coefficients using broom.mixed::tidy().
Visualize your data using the ggeffects::gpredict()
Communicate your analysis in a reproducible Quarto report.

section: Part 1: Configure your project and examine the data
text:
Part 1: Configure your project and examine the data

1.1. Create your project
Create a new GitHub repository for this lab, following the workflow established in Lab 1.
Your repository should contain:

An RStudio project connected to your GitHub repository.
An index.qmd file containing your analysis and written report.
A _quarto.yml file configured to render your report to the docs/ directory.
A docs/ directory containing the rendered website.

Your analysis must be reproducible from the files in your repository.
Important: As in Lab 1, you should distinguish between commands used for interactive exploration in the R Console and commands required to reproduce your results in Quarto.
You may use the Console to inspect datasets, experiment with model specifications, and troubleshoot errors. However, every command necessary to generate the results presented in your report must appear in your Quarto document.


1.2. Load the required packages
You will need the following packages:

dplyr and tidyr for data manipulation.
ggplot2 for visualization.
broom.mixed for extracting binary logistic regression results.
performance for binary logistic regression diagnostics and model comparisons.
gt for formatting tables.
ggeffects for binary logistic regression visualization
glmmTBM for binary logistic regression models.
DHARMa for binary logistic regression diagnostic plots.
titanic for the dataset for today’s lab.

Install any missing packages in the R Console. Load the packages in a setup chunk near the beginning of your Quarto document.


1.3. Load the dataset
We will use the titanic_train dataset from the titanic package. I have adapted this dataset to enhance interpretability and ensure that we are working with the same number of cases for each model. Please run this code below to load the data for this assignment:


Code
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)

titanic <- titanic_train

#Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
titanic <- titanic |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)
 
n <- nrow(titanic)


This dataset contains data on 714 passengers. The binary outcome variable is Survived: whether the passenger survived or died in the Titanic crash. Several other variables summarize characteristics of the Titanic passengers that could influence survival.
For this lab, we will focus on four variables:








Variable
Description
Role


Survived
Whether a passenger survived or died in the crash
Outcome


Sex
Sex reported on legal documents
Predictor


Age
Self-reported age
Predictor


Pclass
What type of ticket was purchased; our proxy for socioeconomic status (SES)
Predictor





1.4. Explore the data
Before estimating any models, familiarize yourself with the variables and their cell counts.
In the R Console:

Inspect the first several observations.
Examine the dataset’s structure.
Calculate descriptive statistics for continuous variables.
Explore the cell counts of the variables.

In your Quarto report:
Include:

A formatted table reporting the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum for the continuous variable.
A formatted table reporting the cell counts for each categorical variable.
A short paragraph describing the most important patterns you observe.

Your discussion should consider whether the cell counts for the categorical variables are evenly distributed and whether the exploratory results are consistent with your expectations.

title: Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
section: Part 2: Specify competing binary logistic regression models
text:
Part 2: Specify competing binary logistic regression models

2.1. Develop your predictions
Before fitting your models, write a short paragraph explaining why you expect the three predictors to be associated with survival of the Titanic crash.
Consider the following questions:

How might gender/sex have influenced how people were treated in emergency situations in 1912?
Could one’s ticket class (our proxy for socioeconomic status [SES]) have influenced who was prioritized in emergency situations?
How might age, particularly whether someone was a child or an adult, have influenced how they were treated in emergency situations?

These predictions should motivate your model specifications.


2.2. Specify four nested models
Estimate the following models:








Model
Predictors
Purpose


mod0: Null
Intercept only
Establish a baseline


mod1: Sex
Sex
Evaluate sex


mod2: Sex + Pclass
Sex, Pclass
Evaluate the additional contribution of ticket class


mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age
Sex, Pclass, Age
Evaluate the additional contribution of age



Use glmmTMG() to estimate each model, assigning each fitted model to a clearly named object.


2.3. Explore your fitted models
In the R Console, use summary() to inspect the results of each fitted model.
Pay particular attention to:

The estimated binary logistic regression coefficients.
The direction and magnitude of predictor associations.
The model AIC and BIC.
How the intercept changes as additional predictors are included.

In your Quarto report, briefly explain how the interpretation of the intercept changes between mod1, mod2, and mod3.
You do not need to reproduce the complete summary() output for every model.

title: Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
Part 3: Compare model performance
You will compare the four models using nested-model χ²-tests and two measures of overall performance.

3.1. Conduct nested-model χ²-tests
Use anova() to compare all four models in a single call, in the order mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3.
The resulting table will allow you to evaluate three questions:

Does Sex explain significantly more variation than the intercept-only model?
Does adding Pclass improve model fit beyond Sex?
Does adding Age increase improve model fit beyond Sex and Pclass?

Retain the following information from the ANOVA results:

Residual degrees of freedom.
Change in degrees of freedom.
χ²-statistic for the nested-model comparison.
p-value for the nested-model comparison.

Use select() and rename() to organize these results into a clearly labelled data frame.


3.2. Extract nested model-level performance statistics
Use broom.mixed::glance() to extract nested model-level statistics for each of the four fitted models.
Combine the results into one data frame using rbind() or bind_rows().
Include a column identifying each model.
For this lab, focus on:

AIC: Evaluates model fit while penalizing model complexity. Lower values indicate a preferred balance between fit and complexity.
BIC: Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity. Lower values are preferred.
Likelihood-ratio test (χ²): Tests whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit relative to the preceding model. A statistically significant p-value (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictors improve model fit.



3.3. Create a combined model-comparison table
Combine the model-performance statistics with the nested-model test results.
You may use cbind() because both sets of results contain the same four models in the same order.
Use gt() to create a professionally formatted table containing:







Column
Meaning


Model
Model identifier


AIC
Evaluates model fit while penalizing model complexity


BIC
Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity.


logLik
Measures how well a model explains the observed data. 


deviance
Measures how poorly a model fits the observed data, relative to a perfectly fitting (saturated) model. Obtained by multiplying the logLik by -2.


Residual df
Residual degrees of freedom


Nested df
Degrees of freedom added by the new predictor(s)


Nested χ²
χ²-statistic comparing the model with its predecessor


Nested p
p-value for the nested comparison



Format the numerical results to an appropriate number of decimal places.


3.4. Interpret the comparisons
Write a paragraph addressing the following:

Which model provides the best fit to the data, considering both model fit and complexity?
How do AIC and BIC change as predictors are added?
Which additions of predictors produce statistically significant improvements in model fit, based on the likelihood-ratio tests?
Do AIC and BIC support the same conclusions as the likelihood-ratio tests? Why or why not?

Explain what the pattern of results suggests about the contribution of each predictor.

title: Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
section: Part 4: Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics
text:
Part 4: Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

4.1. Examine the assumptions
Select the most promising model based on your comparisons in Part 3.
Evaluate the following binary logistic regression assumptions:

Linearity to the logit scale: Is the relationship between predictors and the outcome adequately represented by the model? Is the residual variability reasonably uniform across fitted values? (use DHARMa:: diagnostic plots)
Collinearity: Are predictors so strongly related that their unique contributions may be difficult to estimate precisely?
Complete separation: Does any predictor perfectly predict the outcome variable?
Influential observations: Are there observations that may disproportionately influence the fitted model? (use DHARMa:: again)
Events per predictor: Are there enough events for each coefficient of your predictor variable? 



4.2. Report your diagnostic findings
Include at least one set of diagnostic plots in your Quarto report.
Write a short paragraph explaining:

Which assumptions appear reasonably satisfied.
Whether any potential problems are evident.
Whether those problems affect your confidence in or interpretation of the model.

Avoid treating binary logistic regression assumptions as a mechanical checklist. Explain what the diagnostic results imply for the interpretation of your findings.

title: Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
section: Part 5: Select and report your preferred model
text:
Part 5: Select and report your preferred model

5.1. Select a model
Identify the model you believe provides the most defensible representation of the relationship between surviving the sinking of the Titanic and our passenger-specific variables.
Your decision should consider:

Nested-model χ²-tests.
AIC.
BIC.
Model complexity.
Diagnostic findings.
Substantive interpretability.

You are not required to select the most complex model.
Write a paragraph explaining why your preferred model is more appropriate than the alternatives.


5.2. Create a coefficient table
Use broom.mixed::tidy() to extract the unstandardized binary logistic regression coefficients from your preferred model.
Request 95% confidence intervals.
Use gt() to create a formatted coefficient table containing:

Predictor name.
Unstandardized coefficient estimate.
Standard error.
95% confidence interval.
p-value.

Do not simply paste the output from summary() into your report.


5.3. Interpret the coefficients
Write a paragraph interpreting the binary logistic regression coefficients in your preferred model.
For each included predictor:

Interpret the coefficient on the log-odds scale.
Transform and interpret the coefficients as odds ratios.
Explain what is being held constant when interpreting each predictor in your model.

Use inline R code referencing your tidy() results so that the numerical values in your written interpretation update automatically when the model is re-estimated.
For example, you can use filter() and pull() to retrieve the coefficient estimates, odds ratios, and confidence interval limits for a particular predictor.
You should not manually type coefficient estimates, odds ratios, or confidence intervals into your narrative.


5.4. Report overall model performance
Using gt(), create a table reporting the overall model performance for your preferred model.


5.5. Provide an overarching paragraph summarizing your results
Provide a summary of the analysis you conducted, along with the results of your preferred model (in the metric of odd ratios).


5.6. Visualize one of your predictors using ggeffects
Using ggeffects::ggpredict() and ggplot2, select one predictor from your preferred model and visualize it’s association with the outcome variable, Survived.
